newsitem.title: ITALY: Fujimori vows to clamp down on Peru violence.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori vows to clamp down on Peru violence.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, on his first trip to Europe since sending troops to crush a 126-day siege by Marxist gunmen in Lima, vowed on Monday not to relax efforts to clamp down on guerrilla action.
"I am not going to allow terrorism to rise up again," he told a news conference during a visit to Rome to thank Pope John Paul for spiritual support during the hostage crisis.
"I have not said we have eradicated (terrorism), or finished with it, or decapitated it. It is a process which is still incomplete. But we hope terrorist outbreaks will disappear...
"The Peruvian government is making a heroic effort to change this situation," Fujimori said.

Fujimori earlier met the Pontiff in a private audience at the Vatican to express his "deep thanks for (the Holy Father's) concern" during the four-month crisis in which rebels from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) held 72 hostages.
All 14 rebels were killed when Peruvian troops stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence to end the siege on April 22. One hostage and two commandos also died.
Fujimori, who travelled with six of the former hostages, described the 25-minute meeting with the Pope as "very stimulating" and "spiritually strengthening".
The Vatican, which provided Peruvian Archbishop Luis Cipriani as a mediator between the government and MTRA rebels, issued only a brief statement after the private audience.
"Pope John Paul again expressed his pain for all the victims of the recent events," Chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said.

The bloody end to the siege was potentially embarrassing for the Vatican. Military sources have said the assault was launched with a tip-off via a microphone planted in a crucifix that had been smuggled into the residence.
Fujimori said the Pope shared his concern for Peru's poor and said they had discussed social issues including equality of opportunity, health and access to the justice system.

Poverty still afflicts about half the nation of 24 million, while high unemployment rates and low wage levels have persisted even though Fujimori has succeeded in taming the out-of-control economy he inherited when he took office in 1990.
Many analysts say poor social conditions provide fertile recruiting territory for the MRTA and the other, far larger Maoist Shining Path guerrilla movement.
Fujimori shrugged off criticisms that his government was dictatorial in style. "To call it dictatorial is a long way from reality," he said.
He said his government was working to consolidate democracy, boost a market economy and strengthen social progress.
Fujimori was to meet Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro later on Monday.
